data.title: Evaporative Cooler Covers

internalLinks.label: What Is an Evaporative Cooler Cover?

data.description: Premium custom-fit covers designed specifically for evaporative coolers. Our covers protect your unit from dust, debris, UV damage, and harsh weather conditions year-round. Available in multiple materials, sizes, and configurations to match any cooler type.
data.seoIntro: Evaporative cooler covers shield your unit during the off-season and between cooling cycles, when accumulated dust, falling debris, and prolonged UV exposure cause most premature wear. A properly fitted cover keeps pads, motor, and louvers protected so the unit starts cleanly next season.
seoHighlights: Made-to-measure for down-draft, side-draft, and window units
Heavier 600D fabric option for high-wind regions
Drawstring or elastic hem to prevent wind lift
Optional bottom drainage to avoid trapped moisture

seoFaqs.q: Should I cover my evaporative cooler in winter?
seoFaqs.a: Yes. Off-season covering keeps freezing water out of pads and panels, prevents debris from clogging the float valve, and protects the motor housing from corrosion.

seoFaqs.q: Do I need to drain the cooler before installing a cover?
seoFaqs.a: Always drain the reservoir and let internal components dry for 24 hours before covering. Trapping moisture under a cover encourages rust and mildew.

seoFaqs.q: How do I measure for a custom cover?
seoFaqs.a: Measure width, depth, and height of the cabinet at the widest points, and note the position of any side ducts or top vents so the cover can be cut to clear them.

seoFaqs.q: What fabric weight should I choose?
seoFaqs.a: 300D polyester suits mild climates; 600D or PVC-laminated fabric is recommended for desert sun, coastal salt air, or rooftop installations exposed to constant wind.

seoFaqs.q: Mesh vs vented solid cover?
seoFaqs.a: Mesh is fully breathable. Vented solid covers combine fabric panels with screened ports — better rain resistance with some airflow.

seoFaqs.q: Will the cover trap heat and damage the unit?
seoFaqs.a: No. A correctly sized cover is breathable along the hem and the unit is off when covered. The reflective top panel actually lowers cabinet temperature compared with leaving the unit exposed.

seoFaqs.q: How long does a rooftop cover last?
seoFaqs.a: With UV-stabilized 600D fabric and proper tie-down, expect 4 to 6 seasons of full rooftop exposure before the topcoat degrades. Sheltered installations last considerably longer.

data.title: Cooler Cover Materials Guide
data.description: Compare polyester, canvas, vinyl, mesh, and insulated fabrics for evaporative cooler covers — and choose the right material for your climate and installation.

sections.heading: Polyester (300D–900D Oxford)
sections.body: Polyester is the most common cooler-cover fabric because it balances cost, weight, and weather resistance. Denier (D) indicates thread thickness: 300D is lighter and suited to sheltered installs; 600D is the industry workhorse for residential and light commercial units; 900D canvas-style polyester handles large spans and rooftop exposure.
bullets: PU (polyurethane) coating: water-resistant, good for most dry and mixed climates
UV stabilizers: essential for rooftop and desert sun — pair with our UV-shield products for direct exposure
Typical weight: 0.8–2.0 kg depending on size and denier
Best for: side-draft, down-draft, and standard custom covers where you need durability without vinyl stiffness

sections.heading: Canvas
sections.body: Canvas covers use a heavier woven base (often cotton-poly blend or polyester canvas) with a rugged hand-feel. They resist abrasion and punctures better than light polyester, which matters on industrial sites and rooftop units with sharp flashing or gravel.
bullets: Heavier than 600D polyester — plan for stronger tie-downs on large covers
Often paired with PU or wax-style treatments for water resistance (not fully waterproof without lamination)
Popular on commercial and extra-large cooler covers
Allow extra drying time after rain before storage to prevent mildew on natural-fiber blends

sections.heading: Vinyl & PVC-Backed Fabrics
sections.body: Vinyl and PVC-backed polyester deliver the highest rain protection. Sealed seams and a waterproof rating (e.g. 5000 mm hydrostatic head) keep water out of pads and cabinets during off-season storage. These fabrics are stiffer and louder in wind than oxford polyester.
bullets: Ideal for heavy-rain regions and units left covered through wet seasons
PVC backing adds stiffness — specify split corners or zippers if you need access to disconnect boxes
Anti-mildew treatments recommended for humid climates
See our waterproof premium cover line for fully sealed construction

sections.heading: Mesh
sections.body: High-density polyester mesh blocks leaves, dust, and pests while allowing airflow. Mesh is not a winter cover — use it in-season or in mild climates where condensation under a solid cover is a concern.
bullets: Typical mesh aperture: ~1 mm for debris filtration without starving airflow
Ultra-light (0.3–0.6 kg) — easy on/off during operating season
Pairs well with solid winter covers: mesh in summer, insulated or solid cover in winter
Browse mesh cooler covers for breathable protection options

sections.heading: Insulated Materials
sections.body: Insulated covers add a foam or thermal lining (commonly 3–5 mm) to reduce freeze risk, block drafts, and slow temperature swing inside the cabinet. They are thicker and need slightly larger clearances than uninsulated covers.
bullets: Recommended for winter storage and cold-climate off-season protection
Condensation management: ensure the unit is dry before covering; vented hem designs help
Heavier than standard polyester — use reinforced corners on rooftop units

data.title: Cooler Cover Installation Guide
data.description: How to install evaporative and swamp cooler covers on wall-mount, rooftop, and window units — including wind tie-down and safety checks.

sections.heading: Pre-Installation Checklist
sections.body: Confirm the cooler is off, water drained, and pads are dry. Remove debris from the cabinet top and verify your cover orientation (tagged front/back if applicable). Inspect tie-down straps, drawcords, and grommets before climbing to a rooftop unit.
bullets: Power off at disconnect — never cover a running unit
Drain pan and water lines; dry 24 hours minimum
Clear leaves and grit from the cabinet top
Lay out cover and identify front, back, and opening alignment

sections.heading: Basic Installation Steps
sections.body: Drape the cover over the cabinet starting from the highest point on down-draft units (or from the back on side-draft wall units). Pull the hem evenly around all sides before tightening. Secure the elastic hem or drawcord last so fabric seats flat without twisting.
bullets: Down-draft: align top panel first, then pull skirt down over corners
Side-draft: fit over top, then work hem under bottom flange
Zippered openings: close zippers after hem is positioned
Stand back and check for bunched fabric that can hold water

sections.heading: Rooftop Installation
sections.body: Use fall protection and a helper when possible. Route tie-downs to structural anchors — not loose conduit or pipe straps. Corner webbing on rooftop-grade covers accepts bungee or ratchet straps; avoid overtightening which can tear grommets.
bullets: OSHA-compliant ladder and harness for roof work
Four-point tie-down in high-wind zones
Reflective top panel faces up — verify orientation
Do not trap standing water — confirm drainage grommets are open

sections.heading: Securing in High Winds
sections.body: In sustained winds above 40 mph (64 km/h), use all provided tie-down points and choose 600D or heavier fabric. Cross straps over the top can supplement corner ties on extra-large covers. Inspect after major storms and retighten when fabric relaxes.
bullets: Ratchet straps preferred over single bungees for large commercial covers
Avoid sharp edges — use corner protectors if straps contact metal flashing
Re-tighten 48 hours after first install — fabric relaxes initially
Remove cover before high-wind events if not rated for your exposure class

resources\\installation.mdx.body: Proper installation keeps covers in place through wind and weather without stressing seams. Always shut down and disconnect power before covering, drain the reservoir, and let internal components dry 24 hours to prevent mildew under the fabric.

data.title: Cooler Cover Maintenance Guide
data.description: Clean, store, and repair evaporative cooler covers to extend fabric life — by material type and season.

sections.heading: Regular Cleaning
sections.body: Brush off dry dust monthly during the covered season. Wash once per year (or before off-season storage) with mild soap and cool water — never bleach unless the fabric supplier specifies it. Rinse thoroughly and air-dry fully before folding.
bullets: Polyester / canvas: soft brush + mild detergent, cold water rinse
Vinyl: wipe with damp cloth; avoid petroleum solvents
Mesh: hose down gently; do not machine wash with agitators
Insulated: spot-clean when possible to preserve foam core

sections.heading: Stain Removal
sections.body: Treat bird droppings and sap promptly — they etch coatings if baked in sun. Use a soft cloth and diluted mild detergent; for stubborn marks on vinyl, a dedicated marine/vinyl cleaner is safer than household solvents.
bullets: Act within 48 hours on organic stains
No chlorine bleach on PU-coated polyester
Test cleaner on an inside hem first
Rinse soap residue — it attracts dust when dry

sections.heading: Seasonal Storage
sections.body: Fold loosely along existing creases; do not compress insulated covers under heavy items. Store in a breathable bag or box in a dry, rodent-free space. Silica gel packs help in humid warehouses.
bullets: Ensure cover is 100% dry before bagging
Avoid hot attics above 120°F (49°C) for PVC-backed fabrics
Hang large commercial covers on a rod if folding creases stress seams
Label bag with size and model for faster reinstall next season

sections.heading: Repair Tips
sections.body: Small tears in polyester can be patched with outdoor fabric repair tape or sewn with UV-rated thread. Replace torn grommets rather than pulling straps through ripped holes. Seams showing white PU failure may need professional re-coating or replacement on high-value commercial covers.
bullets: Tape patches: round the corners of patch pieces to prevent peel
Restitch loose hems before they propagate
Replace missing drawcord before wind season
Contact us for bulk repair or replacement on fleet accounts

resources\\maintenance.mdx.body: Covers last longer when cleaned before storage and kept dry between seasons. Mud, bird droppings, and tree sap break down PU coatings over time. Follow material-specific cleaning to avoid stripping waterproof layers or melting heat-transfer logos.

data.title: How to Measure Your Cooler for a Cover
data.description: Step-by-step instructions to measure width, depth, and height of your evaporative cooler for a custom-fit cover — including protrusions and rooftop units.

deepDiveLinks.label: What Is an Evaporative Cooler Cover?

sections.heading: Tools Needed
sections.body: A steel tape measure (preferred over cloth), notepad or phone camera, and optionally a helper for large rooftop units. For down-draft coolers, use a ladder with fall protection and measure from the roof deck to the top of the cabinet.
bullets: Tape measure (ft/in or metric)
Camera — photos speed up custom quotes
Ladder and harness for rooftop units
Model nameplate photo (optional but helpful)

sections.heading: Step 1: Measure Width
sections.body: Width is the longest horizontal side of the cabinet footprint, usually the left-to-right dimension when facing the access panel. Measure at the widest point including corner trim — not across the pad opening inside the hood.
bullets: Measure twice at mid-height and near the top in case the cabinet tapers
Include side flanges or motor humps that extend past the main box
Record in inches to the nearest ¼ in. (or mm)

sections.heading: Step 2: Measure Depth
sections.body: Depth is the front-to-back dimension of the exterior cabinet. On side-draft units mounted to a wall, depth is from the wall surface to the outermost point of the cooler housing (not the pad frame only).
bullets: Account for water lines, float valves, and brackets that project beyond the cabinet
If a pipe exits the side, mark its location for a custom opening
Wall-mount units: measure from the wall to the farthest protrusion

sections.heading: Step 3: Measure Height
sections.body: Height runs from the mounting surface (roof curb or wall bracket base) to the highest point of the cabinet — often a vent cap or lift lid. For down-draft units, include the rain collar if it projects above the roof line.
bullets: Do not compress the measurement if a spring-loaded hood rises above the frame
Flat-top units: add note if water pools — we can specify drainage grommets
Round units: measure height on the straight side, then diameter separately

sections.heading: Step 4: Note Protrusions
sections.body: List every item that breaks the rectangular outline: electrical disconnect boxes, side ducts, overflow drains, service panels, and guy-wire anchors. Custom openings or split corners prevent stretched fabric and torn seams.
bullets: Mark disconnect box location (common on side-draft commercial units)
Photograph all four sides — one missing side causes fit issues
Specify if the cover must clear a locked access door
See common sizing mistakes before you submit your quote request

sizes\\how-to-measure.mdx.body: Accurate measurements prevent gaps that let in dust, wind, and rain. Measure the outside of the metal or plastic cabinet — not the pad, not the internal frame. sections.body: Pad width is smaller than the cabinet. Casters add 3–6 inches stock charts ignore. Averaging three models into one size fits none of them. Custom only works if dimensions reflect the real outside outline.

sections.heading: Solution: Measure Outside at Widest Points
bullets: Width — widest face, including side handles or panel bumps
Depth — include hose ports or panels that stick out past the frame
Height — floor to highest point, casters included
One spreadsheet row per model number — never one "average" row for a mixed fleet

sections.heading: Between Chart Sizes?
sections.body: If you land between stock chart rows, size up — a slightly loose hem with a drawcord fits; a tight cover tears at corners and rides up in wind.

data.title: Custom Opening Designs for Cooler Covers
data.excerpt: Stretched fabric over a hose port, or a flap that won't stay closed in wind? Openings must align with real hardware — send photos and dimensions.

sections.heading: Problem: Cover Fights the Hardware
sections.body: Without cutouts, crews stretch fabric over hose fittings or leave the hem open to reach the panel. Both fail — stretched fabric tears; open hems let wind under the cover.

sections.heading: Solution: Match Opening to Use Case
bullets: Hose connection — reinforced grommet or zip panel at port height
Control panel — Velcro flap for occasional winter access without removing the cover
Fill cap — small zip or snap closure; mark left/right in photos
Include tape measure in photos — we place openings from your dimensions, not guesses

sections.heading: Problem: Condensation in Cold Storage
sections.body: Units sit in freezing equipment yards for months. Temperature swings inside a sealed cover can produce condensation on metal surfaces — even when the unit was shut down correctly.

sections.heading: Solution: Insulated Liner After Proper Shutdown
sections.body: Insulation reduces temperature swing inside a dry, covered cabinet. Prerequisites still apply.

Pads replaced or fully dried before cover goes on
Use only after complete winterizing — see checklist

Unit run with cover installed → overheating risk

sections.body: Rental and event yards lose track of which covers belong to which client. Logo on the side panel at eye height solves identification and doubles as brand visibility on site.

Mixed sizes or full-color logo → heat transfer
Submit vector art (AI/EPS/SVG); high-res PNG works if lines are clean

data.title: Mesh Swamp Cooler Covers
data.excerpt: Pads clogging with yard dust on idle summer units? Mesh keeps debris off while air flows. It will not stop winter drafts, rain, or pests — use solid fabric for shutdown.

sections.heading: Problem: Dust on Idle Units During Cooling Season
sections.body: Portable units sit in gravel yards between jobs. Wind-blown dust loads pads on idle coolers — startup airflow drops and pads need early replacement. Mesh blocks debris while allowing air through.

sections.heading: Solution: Mesh for In-Season Idle Only
bullets: Use when the unit is off but not winterized — still needs airflow
Keeps leaves and dust off pads without trapping heat like solid fabric
Swap to solid winter cover at shutdown — mesh is not a winter product

sections.heading: Do Not Use Mesh When
bullets: Winter shutdown — cold air passes straight through mesh
Rain protection needed — water penetrates openly
Pest blocking — mesh openings are too large for wasps and rodents

data.title: Down Draft Swamp Cooler Covers
data.excerpt: Rain sitting on top of the unit, or top intake still open? Down-draft cabinets need a wide, low cover with a reinforced top — sides alone are not enough.

sections.heading: Problem: Water Pools or Top Intake Exposed
sections.body: Down-draft units pull air through the top deck. Sides are mostly solid. A side-draft cover leaves the primary intake open and may sag in the middle — rainwater pools instead of running off.

sections.heading: Solution: Down-Draft Profile + Drainage
bullets: Wide, low cover shape — top panel is the critical seal
Reinforced top for rain and snow load in open yards
Tighten straps so the top crowns slightly — water runs to edges, not into louvers
Confirm outlet duct clearance before ordering — depth must clear roof connections

sections.heading: Open Yard Storage
sections.body: Add tie-downs on exposed sites. Re-tension after the first storm — a sagging top is the main cause of pooled water and interior rust.

data.title: Side Draft Swamp Cooler Covers
data.excerpt: Cold air still coming in after covering? Side louvers are probably open — you need a tall cover that wraps the intake panels, not a down-draft top-only profile.

sections.heading: Problem: Side Intakes Still Open
sections.body: Side-draft portables pull air through large louvers on the left and right faces. A cover that only seals the top leaves both intakes exposed — drafts and debris get in exactly where you thought you were protected.

sections.heading: Solution: Identify and Wrap Side Draft
sections.body: Large intake louvers on left/right; outlet on top or front.
bullets: Use a side-draft profile — tall enough to wrap both intake faces
Hem below the lowest louver edge, not mid-panel
Route drawcord or strap under the caster frame so wind cannot lift the hem
Do not substitute a down-draft cover — top seal alone fails on side intakes

sections.heading: Still Gaps at Corners?
sections.body: Remeasure outside width and depth — pad dimensions are smaller than the cabinet. Wrong draft type with correct size still leaks.

data.title: Swamp Cooler Cover Sizes

sections.heading: Problem: Chart Size Almost Fits
sections.body: Stock charts list outside dimension ranges. Landing between two rows is common — especially when casters add height the chart does not show. Ordering down saves money once; reordering after a failed fit costs a season.

sections.heading: Solution: Size Up, Then Adjust Hem
bullets: Measure outside W×D×H at widest points — casters included
Between rows → pick the next size up; drawcord or strap takes up slack
Hem should sit below the lowest louver, not above casters
Still tight at hose ports → custom pattern, not the next stock size

sections.heading: When Stock Will Not Work
bullets: Rear hose panel sticks out past cabinet depth
Three models in one yard — no single chart row fits all
Control panel on the face breaks a flat rectangle

data.title: UV Protection for Cooler Covers
data.excerpt: Cover faded and tore at the hem in one season? Southwest sun destroys low-denier fabric — specify 600D+ with UV-stabilized coating and expect shorter life on exposed rooftops.

sections.heading: Problem: One-Season Fabric Failure
sections.body: High-desert UV breaks down cheap polyester fast — especially at hem contact points and anywhere the fabric rubs on casters or roof curbs. Fading is the visible sign; brittleness and tearing at stress points follow in the same season.

sections.heading: Solution: Spec for UV Exposure
bullets: 600D or higher polyester with UV-stabilized PU or vinyl coating
Darker colors fade slower than light colors on exposed sites
Rooftop and open yard storage → shortest lifespan; inspect hems yearly
Store folded in shade between seasons when possible

sections.heading: When to Replace vs Repair
sections.body: Small hem fraying on an otherwise sound cover → repair tape or patch. Widespread brittleness or coating breakdown → replace — UV damage is through the fabric, not just the surface.

data.title: Vented vs Closed Cooler Covers
data.excerpt: Still cold indoors with a cover on, or pads got wet under a "breathable" cover in winter? Mesh and vented fabrics are for in-season idle only — winter needs solid closure.

sections.heading: Problem: Wrong Closure for the Season
sections.body: Mesh keeps dust off idle summer units while air flows. Used at winter shutdown, cold outdoor air passes straight through — drafts continue and rain soaks pads. Teams sometimes pick mesh because it is lighter and cheaper; the failure shows up as cold rooms and wet pads in spring.

sections.heading: Solution: Closed for Shutdown, Vented for Idle
bullets: Closed solid fabric — after full drain/dry shutdown; blocks drafts, rain, and pests
Mesh / vented — idle unit during cooling season in dusty yards; not winter
At shutdown: swap mesh for solid cover — do not leave mesh on through winter

sections.heading: Interior Duct Still Drafting?
sections.body: A solid cover seals outdoor intakes only. If rooms stay cold, check the interior duct damper or panel inside the house — cover fabric cannot fix an open duct path.

data.title: Waterproof vs Water-Resistant Cooler Covers
data.excerpt: Water inside the cabinet after a storm? PU-coated polyester sheds rain but stitched seams wick under standing water — vinyl is required when puddles form on top.

sections.heading: Problem: Dry Climate Fabric, Wet Climate Install
sections.body: 600D PU polyester is the right default for dry Southwest winters — light rain beads off. On a rooftop where water pools after storms, or in coastal exposure, prolonged standing water wicks through stitched seams. Interior rust follows even when the cover "looks fine" from the ground.

sections.heading: Solution: Match to Worst Case, Not Average
bullets: Water-resistant (600D PU) — dry climates, wall mounts, light rain only
Waterproof (vinyl-coated) — rooftop ponding, heavy snow load, coastal rain
If you see puddles on top after storms → upgrade to vinyl regardless of climate zone

sections.heading: Also Fix Drainage
sections.body: Wrong fabric is not the only cause of interior wet — a sagging top pools water even on vinyl. Crown the top with strap tension so runoff reaches edges.

data.title: What Is an Evaporative Cooler Cover?
data.excerpt: Open intakes let cold air, rain, and pests in all winter. A cover seals the cabinet from the outside — but only after you drain and dry the unit.

sections.heading: Problem: Open Intakes All Winter
sections.body: Evaporative coolers need large intake panels to pull air through wet pads in summer. When the unit is off, those same openings become a straight path for cold outdoor air, rain, dust, and nesting pests. A tarp thrown over the top usually leaves side gaps — a fitted cover wraps the outside cabinet and closes every intake path.

sections.heading: Solution: Match Cover Profile to Your Unit
sections.body: Wrong type = gaps even when the size looks close. Identify your cooler first.
bullets: Side draft — tall cover; side louvers must be fully wrapped
Down draft — wide, low profile; top deck is the intake to seal
Rooftop — reinforced top + tie-downs; water must drain off, not into the curb
Window — frame-width fit; blocks the window opening from drafting

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
bullets: Running the cooler with the cover on → overheating and motor damage
Covering a unit that still has water in the pan → rust and mold under the fabric
Using a down-draft cover on a side-draft unit → side intakes stay open

data.title: Winterizing Your Evaporative Cooler
data.excerpt: Mold smell in spring or a cracked water line? You skipped shutdown steps. Drain, dry, seal the interior duct — then install the cover last.

sections.heading: Problem: Covering Too Early or While Wet
sections.body: A cover on a wet unit traps moisture → rust, mold, and pad rot by spring. Shut down when nights stay below ~50°F and you will not need cooling again until spring. The cover is the last step, not a substitute for draining.

sections.heading: Solution: Shutdown Checklist
sections.body: Do these in order. Cleaning detail and storage tips are in the maintenance guide.
bullets: Power off at the disconnect — not just the wall switch
Close the water valve; disconnect and blow out the feed line
Drain the pan completely; leave the drain plug open
Scrub the pan; inspect pads — replace damaged ones or dry fully before covering
Seal the interior duct opening inside the house (damper or insulated panel)
Install cover — correct draft type, hem below lowest louver, tie-downs if exposed

sections.heading: If You Already Have These Symptoms
bullets: Mold smell when you remove the cover → unit was wet; drain and dry fully next season
Cracked feed line in spring → line was still full of water when it froze
Still cold indoors → interior duct not sealed — cover alone does not fix in-house draft
Cover on the ground after a storm → add tie-downs; see installation guide
